title: Always override toString
concept: While java.lang.Object provides an implementation of toString, it simply returns the class name followed by an '@' sign and the hexadecimal hash code (e.g. PhoneNumber@163b91). A concise, informative toString makes your class far more pleasant to use and vastly easier to debug in log files, debugger watches, and test assertions. When practical, toString should return all of the interesting information contained in the object. Whether or not you specify the exact format in documentation, clearly document your intent and provide programmatic access (getters) to all data contained in the return value.

when_to_use_flashcard.front: When should you override toString() in a Java class?
when_to_use_flashcard.back: In virtually every instantiable class (especially value classes). Only static utility classes and enum types (which already provide good toString implementations) typically don't need it.

when_not_to_use_flashcard.front: What must you always provide alongside a detailed toString() method?
when_not_to_use_flashcard.back: Programmatic access (getters) to all information contained in the string, so callers aren't forced to parse the string to retrieve individual fields.

quiz.question: What is the default implementation of `Object.toString()` in Java?
options: The class name followed by '@' and the unsigned hexadecimal representation of the object's hash code
A JSON representation of the object's fields
An empty string
The memory address of the object in native C pointers

quiz.question: What is a major trade-off of specifying an exact, standardized format in Javadoc for a value class's `toString()`?
options: Clients will write parsers against the format, locking you into that format forever even if internal representations change
It prevents the class from implementing Serializable
The compiler enforces format checks at compile-time
It slows down garbage collection

quiz.question: Why must you provide programmatic access (getters) to all data represented in `toString()`?
options: To prevent programmers from writing brittle string-parsing code that breaks when the format changes
Because Java reflection requires public getters
To allow toString() to run on a background thread
It is required by the equals contract

quiz.question: Which types of classes generally do NOT need custom `toString()` overrides?
options: Static utility classes (which are noninstantiable) and enum types (which have built-in names)
Collections and Maps
Value classes like BigInteger or Date
Java Records

quiz.question: How do modern Java Records (Java 16+) handle `toString()`?
options: They automatically generate a clean toString() showing the record name and all component names with values
They inherit Object.toString()
They return an XML string
Records disallow overriding toString()

interview_questions.question: Why is a good `toString()` implementation critical for developer productivity and operations?
interview_questions.model_answer: When an object is passed to `println()`, `printf()`, string concatenation (`+`), logging frameworks (SLF4J/Logback), debugger inspection panes, or test assertion failures (`assertEquals`), `toString()` is automatically called. A diagnostic, human-readable string drastically accelerates debugging and triage.

interview_questions.question: A class has `toString()` returning `"Person[name=" + name + ", age=" + age + "]"`, but has no `getAge()` method. What design flaw does this introduce?
interview_questions.model_answer: It forces developers who need the age to parse the `toString()` output with regex or string splitting. This creates brittle, error-prone client code that crashes if formatting or spacing ever changes in the future. Always provide getters for any data exposed in `toString()`.

interview_questions.question: Should sensitive user information (like passwords, credit cards, or SSNs) be included in `toString()`?
interview_questions.model_answer: No! `toString()` is frequently printed to application logs, crash reports, and error traces. Exposing sensitive data in `toString()` is a classic security vulnerability and compliance violation (PCI-DSS/GDPR). Sensitive fields must be masked (e.g. `"card=****-****-****-1234"`) or excluded entirely.

interview_questions.question: How do libraries like Google AutoValue or Project Lombok assist with `toString()`?
interview_questions.model_answer: They automatically generate consistent, null-safe `toString()` methods at compile time based on class fields, eliminating boilerplate and guaranteeing that newly added fields are included in string representations without human oversight.
